chapter.title: Twelve Minutes
chapter.sub: Captions on air, none on the stream — for twelve minutes of a road-closure bulletin.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the owner's request to continue the story · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 4 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT  Accessibility · Maya and June · Level L3  For twelve minutes last night, deaf viewers on the stream didn’t see the Route 9 closure. The captioner typed every word. Somewhere, the words were thrown away.  ⚑ RV-89: caption transport simplified. RV-81: Deaf and hard-of-hearing representation. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Twelve Minutes
items.stakes: Deaf viewers on the stream missed a road-closure bulletin. One of them was Dolores. She drove to the barrier before she found out. She's eighty-one.
items.reward: Captions on every path, proven with the person who knows. June's respect — which you have to earn.

objectives.text: Find the missing captions without blaming the captioner
Route the stream through a profile that keeps captions
Prove it the way June would
Look closer: two people who noticed

items.rumor: The profile that ate the captions has a name. Somebody applied it on a Saturday and called it 'quality'.

items.alt: A living room up the valley. On the TV, streaming: a bulletin card, Route 9 closed. The caption bar is empty. Dolores leans toward the screen, hearing aid in, catching nothing.
items.caption: 10:14 p.m. The bulletin is on screen. The words aren't.

items.alt: Night, rain, headlights on an orange barrier across Route 9: ROAD CLOSED. Beyond it, the dark shine of water where the road should be.
narration: Seventeen minutes after the bulletin, Dolores's headlights find the barrier. She reads it twice. Then she turns around, very slowly, in the rain.
items.caption: The barrier knew before she did.

items.alt: The next morning. June at her desk, on a video call with Dolores.

bubbles.text: I turned around. I'm fine. I just didn't know.

items.caption: Dolores missed it. She's fine. This time.

lines.text: I'm fine. I turned around at the barrier. I'm eighty-one, June. I shouldn't have been out there at all.
You shouldn't have had to find out from a barrier.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #35 · AVERY'S LENS  Test the path the person uses  Accessibility is proven on the output the person actually uses — not on the one that's easiest to check.  Captions were checked on broadcast every night. Deaf viewers on the stream had none for twelve minutes, and nobody's monitor showed it.

items.alt: June in master control, arms folded, facing Maya.

bubbles.text: Twelve minutes. Everyone's first question is going to be about my encoder.
Mine's about where the words stopped. Can I see your log?

items.prompt: Say it. You think it was my encoder. Everyone thinks it's the captioner first.

options.label: “I think your log will tell us. Can I see it?”
options.reply: …Finally. Someone asks for the log before the apology.

options.label: “It might be. Let's restart it and see.”
options.reply: Touch my encoder and you lose my proof. No.

items.prompt: 9:12. The late news is tonight. What's your first move?
items.happening: Captions missing on the stream for 12 min last night. Broadcast looked fine.
items.risk: Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, during emergency bulletins.
timeout: Lena, hearing nothing, restarts June's encoder 'to be safe.'
If you don't choose the evidence, someone else will erase it.

hints.text: What proves the captions left the captioner?

options.label: Restart June's caption encoder to clear any fault
options.consequence: The one record that clears the captioner is erased — and she knows you thought it was her.
options.fail: Her encoder was the part that worked. You destroyed its proof.

options.label: Ask June to re-caption last night's bulletin live now
options.result: June: “I'll do it. It'll vanish again.”
options.consequence: The captioner treated as the fault; the path unchanged.
options.fail: It fixes nothing and puts the work back on the person who did it right.

options.label: Ask for June's log, check broadcast, then watch the stream from a phone off the network
options.result: Log: every word sent. Broadcast: captions throughout. Stream on a phone: none.
options.consequence: In ten minutes the captioner is cleared and the stream path is the suspect.

options.label: Tell Vera captions are a nice-to-have for tonight
options.consequence: You'll never be trusted with access again — and shouldn't be.
options.fail: For deaf viewers, captions are the bulletin.

items.alt: June's caption encoder log: every line sent from 22:14 to 22:26 — Route 9 is closed between Old Mill and Cedar Row, use… — nineteen hundred more lines, back to you, Omar.
items.caption: Every word left her desk.

items.title: A second screen, always on the stream
items.body: She watches her own captions on the stream while she types them — has for three years. Last night her second screen was showing a documentary about glaciers. Her mother was visiting. The one night she didn't check.

items.title: She sent every word.
items.body: June's log and the broadcast recording agree: the captions left her encoder and reached broadcast perfectly. Whatever threw them away sits on the stream path alone — downstream of the split, in a box nobody watches for captions.
items.label: Test: what does this rule out?

items.alt: A split panel. Left, what hearing viewers got: a sound wave and the words 'Route 9 is closed between Old Mill and Cedar Row. Use the county road.' Right, what Dolores got: the same picture, an empty caption bar, twelve minutes, zero words.
items.caption: Same bulletin. Same minute. Two different nights.

items.title: Captions on the air
items.body: In March 1980, closed captions — text hidden in the television signal and shown only by viewers with a decoder — began appearing on scheduled national U.S. broadcasts. Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers had campaigned for years for access to news and entertainment. Live captioning of news, typed in real time, followed soon after. The principle hasn't changed: the words travel with the picture, and every box in between has to carry them.

items.alt: System View: June's captions and the program video meet at the caption inserter; the broadcast chain passes caption data; the stream path runs through transcoder profile SPORTS TEST, which discards ancillary data. Monitoring checks captions on broadcast only.
items.caption: Picture perfect. Sound perfect. Captions: gone.

lines.text: Hearing people think captions are a nice extra. For me they're the audio. For Dolores they're the road.
(Maya thinks of AUX 4, and nine years of readings nobody heard.)

items.alt: The stream transcoder's profile page: SPORTS TEST, ancillary data discard, since Saturday 13:02; change record says stream quality, vendor.
items.caption: A weekend test, never rolled back. The record said 'quality'. It didn't say 'captions'.

items.title: “Sports mode A/B — revert Mon (probably)”
items.body: The engineer on the vendor side meant to roll it back. They went on leave on Monday. *(probably)* is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

items.title: It was called “quality.”
items.body: On Saturday a vendor's remote session switched the stream to a sports-mode test profile. The change record said 'stream quality improvements'. Nobody reading it would think of captions — and the profile threw them away. It's warning #9 on the wall: nobody monitors captions on the stream.
items.label: Test: what rule would have caught it?

items.alt: The vendor's automatic reply on a master-control screen: on leave until Monday; for urgent matters please contact my colleague, who is also on leave. Maya and June read it with identical expressions.
items.caption: The system is working exactly as designed. Nobody designed it for tonight.

items.prompt: 11:10. The vendor is out until Monday. The late news is tonight. What do you do?
timeout: The decision drifts to 'after lunch', then 'Monday'.
Access problems wait longest when nobody owns them.

options.label: Wait for the vendor — it's their profile
options.result: Tonight's late news runs without captions on the stream.
options.consequence: Deaf viewers pay for a calendar.
options.fail: The stream chain is the station's to run. The vendor can be told, not waited for.

options.label: Roll the stream back to the NEWS profile now, tell the vendor why, and verify from a phone
options.result: Captions return on the stream within a minute.

options.label: Turn the stream off tonight to be safe
options.result: Stream viewers get nothing — captions or not.
options.consequence: You fixed access by removing the service.
options.fail: Removing the service removes access too.

options.label: Ask June to type into the stream's chat box instead
options.result: June: “Into a chat. During an emergency.”
options.consequence: A workaround that puts the burden back on June and on viewers.

items.alt: System View after the rollback: the stream now runs through the NEWS profile, which passes caption data, and caption-present monitoring covers every output.
items.caption: Every path carries the words.

items.label: **Fix it:** route the stream through a profile that keeps captions.

items.alt: A phone off the station network shows the stream with captions: Route 9 closed. June points at it.
items.caption: Proof where Dolores watches — confirmed by the person who knows.

lines.text: Don't get sentimental. Get the alarm on every output.

items.alt: June lines up two more devices: a TV app and an old tablet, both on the stream, both showing captions. She's not smiling yet.

bubbles.text: One phone isn't 'every path.' Dolores uses the TV app. Her neighbour uses a tablet older than Tess.

items.caption: June's rule: test the path the person actually uses — all of them.

items.prompt: The captions are back. What do you set up before tonight?
timeout: The day ends with the fix and no alarm.
Fixed isn't safe until something tells you when it breaks.

options.label: A caption-present alarm on every output, test profiles that roll back automatically, and June on the approval list for any stream change
options.result: June: “Put me on the list. I'll read every one.”
options.consequence: Access gets a monitor and an owner.

options.label: Ask June to keep a second screen on the stream forever
options.result: June: “I type 200 words a minute. I can't also be your monitor.”
options.consequence: A person as the only alarm.
options.fail: People aren't monitoring systems — especially the one doing the job.

options.label: Nothing — it's fixed
options.fail: The same path can fail the same way tomorrow.

options.label: Ban all vendor changes
options.result: The vendor can't fix the encoder next month either.
options.consequence: A wall instead of a door.

items.alt: Dolores at home watching the late news on the stream, captions showing: the Old Mill gauge is rising.
items.caption: The captions are back. So is the river.

lines.text: Tell June I read every word tonight.
And tell her the river's in the words now. The gauge man said 'rising' twice.

items.alt: After the late news. June has taken her headset off and sits with her hands flat on the desk. Maya sits nearby and says nothing.

bubbles.text: Twelve minutes. I'll count them for a year. I'll count them when I'm eighty-one.

narration: Maya doesn't say it's not her fault. June knows that. That isn't the part that hurts.
items.caption: Some silences are the right answer.

items.alt: Cal's warnings on the wall; June herself crosses out number nine.
items.caption: Warning #9: crossed off — by June.

items.alt: Night at the mountain transmitter site in a storm: wind streaks, rain, the tower in the distance with its red beacon. Felix, hard hat and vest, on a radio, standing by the building, far from the tower.

bubbles.text: Channel's off the air. Wind's at seventy up here. Nobody's climbing anything.

items.caption: Next: *The Mountain.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  When captions vanish on one output, clear the captioner with her log, compare outputs, and look for the box that changed on the failing path. Roll it back tonight, verify from where deaf viewers watch — with the person who knows — and alarm on caption presence at every output.
REFLECTION (optional)  · The one night June didn't watch her own captions was the night they vanished. What are you the only alarm for?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't monitor anything.
